title: Leases, locks and fencing tokens
goal: By the end, you can build a lock in Redis that never deletes another server's lock, explain why a lock that runs out can't stop a frozen holder from writing, even in a stronger lock service, and make the thing being written refuse a late writer with a fencing token.
opening:
Every night, the payments company pays each shop what it took that day. One job builds the payout file, a list that tells the bank how much to send to each shop, and it must run exactly once. Run it twice, and every shop is paid twice.

The job runs on three servers, so that one dying on the night doesn't stop the payouts. The tempting fix is a lock: before it starts, a server takes a lock that only one may hold, and the others wait. Every programmer trusts locks, because inside one program nobody can take a lock away from you while you hold it.

In Process pauses, a worker checked its lease, froze for 3 seconds, and wrote after the lease had run out. A lock shared by three servers has to run out too, so it has the same gap. In this lesson, we'll build that lock in Redis, break it three ways, and fix it at the one place that sees every write. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: Server A takes a lock with a 10-second deadline, then freezes for 15 seconds, for any of the reasons in Process pauses. Meanwhile server B takes the lock and writes the payout file. Which change stops A from overwriting B's file when it wakes up?
options: Release the lock with a command that deletes it only if it's still A's
Move the lock from Redis to etcd, a lock service that keeps every change on several machines
Raise the deadline to 60 seconds
Make the file store refuse writes that carry an older lock number than one it has already seen
warmup.why: The freeze happens after A got the lock, so nothing on the lock service's side can stop A from writing when it wakes: A doesn't know its lock ran out. Deleting only your own lock stops A from deleting B's, not from writing. etcd keeps the lock safe if one of its machines crashes, not from a holder that froze after taking it; a test of etcd 3.4.3 lost about 18% of the updates its locks were meant to protect. A longer deadline only needs a longer freeze. Only the file store sees both writes, so only it can refuse the late one, if each write carries a number that grows with every new lock holder. That number is a fencing token, the subject of the fourth section.

sections.h: A lock in Redis, and the deadline that makes it dangerous
sections.body:
Let's build the lock. Inside one program, a lock is a simple thing. Java's `synchronized` and `ReentrantLock` let one thread (one line of work in a program) at a time into a piece of code, and the others wait at the door. That works because all the threads share the program's memory, where the lock lives. Our three servers share no memory. (The commands below call them `pod-a`, `pod-b` and `pod-c`; here they're servers A, B and C.) So the lock has to live somewhere all three can reach.

Redis is a good first place. It's a program that keeps data in memory and answers many programs at once, and each piece of data sits under a name, called a key. Redis runs one command at a time, from start to end (Inside an in-memory store: how Redis executes commands). So a command that creates a key only if it doesn't exist yet is a perfect "first one wins". `SET lock:settle pod-a NX` stores the value `pod-a` under the key `lock:settle`, and `NX` means "only if the key doesn't exist". Exactly one server gets the answer `OK`; the others get nil, Redis's word for nothing. Holding the lock means the key exists, and releasing it is `DEL`, which deletes the key.

That breaks the first time a holder dies. Server A crashes halfway through the job, the key stays forever, and no server ever runs the job again. So the lock needs a deadline: `SET lock:settle pod-a NX PX 30000`. `PX 30000` tells Redis to delete the key by itself after 30,000 ms. That deadline is the key's TTL, its time to live (Expiry, eviction and memory). It has to be part of the same command: sent as a second command, a crash in between leaves a key with no deadline, the trap from Rate limiting and idempotency keys. A lock with a deadline is a **lease**, the thing the workers in Process pauses kept renewing.

The deadline is what makes the lock work, and what makes it dangerous. Redis deletes the key after 30 seconds whether or not the holder has finished, and nothing tells the holder. Suppose the job runs slower than usual, or server A freezes for 35 seconds. The lease runs out. Server B's `SET NX` succeeds, and B starts the job too. Then A finishes and runs `DEL lock:settle`, which deletes B's lock, not A's. Server C's `SET NX` succeeds while B is still running. Three servers have run a job that must run once, and every step looked correct from where it ran.

That's the picture for the whole lesson, and it holds for every lock service, not only Redis. A lease is a record of who may act, until a deadline. **The lock service enforces the deadline. Nothing makes the holder stop when it passes.** Each of the next sections deals with one result of that, starting with the delete that removed someone else's lock.

aside.title: Why not run the job on one server?
aside.body: You could, and some teams do. Then on the night that server is down, or being replaced, nobody pays the shops until a person notices and starts the job somewhere else. Three servers that compete for a lock fix that by themselves: whichever one is alive takes the lock. The price is the rest of this lesson, making sure that only one of them acts.

try.title: Let a lease run out, then delete the wrong lock
steps: This needs Docker. From the `labs` folder, start Redis with `docker compose -f env/redis.yml up -d` if it isn't running. Then open two Redis prompts with `docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli`, one for server A and one for server B.

Server A clears any lock left from an earlier run and takes the lock with a 10-second lease. Server B tries at once, and checks how long the lock has left with `PTTL`. Then wait at least 10 seconds: A is "frozen".
Server B tries again. Then server A, which knows nothing about its freeze, releases with `DEL`. Finally a third server tries (use B's prompt). Predict every reply first.

code.title: two prompts (lines starting with # are notes)
code.src:
# pod A
DEL lock:settle
SET lock:settle pod-a NX PX 10000
# pod B
SET lock:settle pod-b NX PX 10000
PTTL lock:settle
# wait 10 seconds: A's lease runs out while A is "paused"
PTTL lock:settle
SET lock:settle pod-b NX PX 30000
# pod A wakes up and releases its lock
DEL lock:settle
# pod B (playing pod C)
SET lock:settle pod-c NX PX 30000
GET lock:settle

try.expect: The first `DEL` prints `(integer) 0`, or 1 if an earlier run left the key behind. A's SET prints `OK` and B's first SET prints `(nil)`; `PTTL` shows a little under 10000, the milliseconds left. After the wait, `PTTL` prints `(integer) -2`: the key is gone. B's SET prints `OK`, so B now holds the lock. A's `DEL` prints `(integer) 1`: it deleted B's lock, and A can't tell from the reply. Server C's SET prints `OK` while B is still "working", and `GET` shows `"pod-c"`.

sections.h: Release only your own lock, in one command
sections.body:
To stop A from deleting B's lock, each lock must say whose it is. So every time a server takes the lock, it stores a fresh random value that only it knows, a **lock token**: `SET lock:settle 6f1e... NX PX 30000`. A random UUID, a 128-bit id with 122 random bits, is plenty; the Redis docs suggest 20 random bytes. The server's name won't do. One server can take the lock twice in a row, and its old attempt and its new one would look the same.

The first release that comes to mind has three steps: GET the key, compare it with my token in my own code, and DEL if they match. It's a check-then-act: a check, then a separate act, with room for a pause in between, as in Process pauses. The Transactions track met the same race (Serial execution: Redis MULTI, WATCH and Lua). A reads its own token. Then A freezes, say for a garbage collection, when the JVM (the program that runs Java and Kotlin code) stops every thread to free memory (Process pauses). A's lease runs out, and B takes the lock. Then A's DEL arrives and deletes B's lock after all. The simulator below lets you play exactly that; it calls the servers Pod A and Pod B.

The compare and the delete have to be one command. Redis can run a small script, written in a language called Lua, as one command, and nothing else runs in the middle of it. This is the script from the Redis docs:

```text
if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
    return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1])
end
return 0
```

It returns 1 when it deleted my lock, and 0 when the key holds someone else's token, or doesn't exist. Redis 8.4 made it a single built-in command: `DELEX lock:settle IFEQ <token>`, delete if equal. In Jedis, the Java library the labs use to talk to Redis, that's `redis.delex(key, CompareCondition.valueEq(token))`. Extending a lease needs the same care, because it must only push out my own deadline: `SET lock:settle <token> IFEQ <token> PX 30000` on Redis 8.4, or a script that compares the token before it sets the new deadline.

Two other lock services, etcd and ZooKeeper, avoid this mistake by design. Both are programs built to hold locks and small settings for other programs. In their lock recipes, every waiting client (a program using the service) creates its own key, the oldest key holds the lock, and a client only ever deletes its own. In Redis, you build the check yourself.

Be clear about what this fixes. A can no longer delete B's lock, so C can't get in while B works. But A and B both still ran the job: A's lease ran out while A was working, and no release can undo that. Next, we'll see whether renewing the lease can stop that from happening.

sim.title: Pod A releases with GET, compare, then DEL
sim.intro: lock = 1 means the key holds A's token, 2 means B's token, 0 means there is no key. A releases the slow way: three steps. Can you make A delete B's lock?

steps.code: GET lock:settle == tok-A? (if not: stop, it isn't mine)
full GC: the JVM stops for 12 s
(10 s later) A's lease ends: Redis deletes the key
SET lock:settle tok-B NX PX 10000 (only if no key)
OK: B holds the lock and starts the batch

goal.say: A deleted B's lock. A's GET saw its own token, then A paused; by the time its DEL arrived, the key held B's token. B is still running the batch and the key is gone, so any pod's SET NX succeeds now. Inside one script, nothing can run between the compare and the delete.

try.title: Release by token, with a script and with DELEX
steps: At a Redis prompt (`docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli`), clear the key, then let server B take the lock with token `tok-b-6f1e`.
Play server A's late release with the script and A's old token, then read the key. Then try `DELEX` (Redis 8.4) with A's token and with B's.
Take the lock as server C with a 2-second lease and extend it with `SET ... IFEQ`. Then try to extend it with A's token.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.src:
DEL lock:settle
SET lock:settle tok-b-6f1e NX PX 30000
EVAL "if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) end return 0" 1 lock:settle tok-a-91c2
GET lock:settle
DELEX lock:settle IFEQ tok-a-91c2
DELEX lock:settle IFEQ tok-b-6f1e
SET lock:settle tok-c-0d77 NX PX 2000
SET lock:settle tok-c-0d77 IFEQ tok-c-0d77 PX 30000
PTTL lock:settle
SET lock:settle tok-a-91c2 IFEQ tok-a-91c2 PX 30000

try.expect: The first `DEL` prints `(integer) 0`, or 1 if an earlier run left the key behind. The SET prints `OK`. The script prints `(integer) 0`, and `GET` still shows `"tok-b-6f1e"`: A's late release left B's lock alone. `DELEX ... IFEQ tok-a-91c2` prints `(integer) 0`, and `DELEX ... IFEQ tok-b-6f1e` prints `(integer) 1`. C's SET prints `OK`, the extend prints `OK`, and `PTTL` shows `(integer) 29999` or close: the 2-second lease is now 30 seconds. Extending with A's token prints `(nil)` and changes nothing.

sections.h: Renewing the lease, and why a stronger lock service doesn't help
sections.body:
How long should the lease be? Too short, and a slow job outlives it. Too long, and a crashed holder blocks everyone until it ends: with a 10-minute lease, a server that dies one second in holds up the job for 9 minutes 59 seconds.

The usual answer is to keep the lease short and renew it while the work runs, as the workers in Process pauses did. Redisson, a Java library that builds locks and other tools on top of Redis, does this for you with a background thread it calls the **watchdog**. Its lock, `RLock`, taken with `lock()` and no lease time, gets a lease of `lockWatchdogTimeout`, 30 seconds by default. The watchdog keeps extending it while the program that took it runs. In the Try it, with the timeout set to 3 seconds, the lock's time to live stayed between about 2,000 and 3,000 ms for 4 seconds. The watchdog put it back to 3,000 about once a second, a third of the timeout. With a fixed lease, `lock.lock(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)`, there is no watchdog, and the key was gone after 2 seconds whether or not the work was done.

Renewal narrows the gap. It doesn't close it. The watchdog is a thread in the same JVM. A stop-the-world pause, which stops every thread, stops it too, and so does every other cause from Process pauses. Checking "do I still hold it?" right before each write doesn't save you either. That lesson's sweep showed that a second check cuts late writes about 14 times, and leaves the ones whose pause starts after it.

What about a stronger lock service? etcd and ZooKeeper each run on several machines and use consensus, a way for machines to agree on every change, so that one crashed machine loses nothing. (A Redis copy can lose a lock in a crash, as the last section shows, and the Consistency and consensus track builds consensus.) But their locks are leases too. An etcd lock key is attached to a lease that the client keeps alive. A ZooKeeper lock is a key that disappears when the client's session, its connection kept alive by regular messages, times out. A frozen client stops its messages like any other.

Jepsen, a project that tests databases by breaking them on purpose, tested etcd 3.4.3 in 2020. Its ordinary reads and writes stayed correct through pauses, crashes, clock jumps and a network that cut the machines apart. Its locks did not keep holders apart, even when the cluster, the group of etcd machines, was healthy. With leases of 1 to 3 seconds, two clients held one lock at the same time within minutes. A set of values guarded by an etcd lock, with 2-second leases, five clients and a pause every 5 seconds, lost about 18% of its confirmed updates. An etcd bug made it worse: a waiting client was given the lock without a check that its lease was still alive (fixed after 3.4.3). But no fix to the service can stop a client that freezes after it got the lock. Jepsen's advice was to use etcd locks to save work, and to fence every write with the lock key's revision. The next section says what that means.

try.title: Watch Redisson's watchdog renew a lease
steps: With Redis running, run `WatchdogDemo` (Java) or `WatchdogDemoKt` (Kotlin) from the `labs` folder. It takes about 8 seconds. The demo sets `lockWatchdogTimeout` to 3 seconds so the renewals are easy to see.
Read the first PTTL line: the lock's time to live, read every 500 ms. What is the lowest value, and how often does it jump back up?

Read the second line, with a fixed 2-second lease. Then run the demo again and compare the two fencing tokens at the end with the first run's. (Fencing tokens are the next section's subject; for now, watch what happens to the numbers.)

code.title: WatchdogDemo.java

alt.title: WatchdogDemo.kt

try.expect: The first line shows a hash, a Redis value with named fields, such as `{7aadc447-...:3=1}`. The field is the Redisson client's id and the thread's id, and the value counts how many times that thread holds the lock: once. The PTTL readings rise and fall like the teeth of a saw, for example `2418 2954 2432 2955 2451 2957 2451 2956`. They never fall far below 2,000 ms, because the watchdog resets the lease to 3,000 about every second. With `lock(2, SECONDS)` they count down, `1494 987 484 -2 -2 -2`: no renewals, the key is gone after 2 seconds, and `isHeldByCurrentThread()` is `false`. The fencing tokens are `1, 2` on the first run and `3, 4` on the next: the counter lives in Redis and keeps growing.

refs.title: How to do distributed locking (Martin Kleppmann)

sections.h: Fencing tokens let the thing being written refuse a late holder
sections.body:
If the holder can't know that its lease ended, someone else has to refuse its late writes. The only party that sees every write is the thing being written, which this lesson calls the resource: the store that keeps the payout file, a database table, the bank's own system.

That takes one more number. Each time a server takes the lock, it also gets a **fencing token**, a number that grows with every new holder: 33 for A, 34 for B. Every write to the resource carries the token. The resource remembers the highest token it has accepted and refuses any write with a lower one. When A wakes from its freeze and writes with 33 after B has written with 34, the write is refused.

It works like the ticket numbers at a deli counter. Once the counter has served number 34, a customer who turns up late holding 33 is sent away, however sure they are that it's their turn. The ticket is the token, and the counter is the resource. The picture breaks in one place. The deli calls each number itself, so it knows when 34 is being served. The resource learns about 34 only when B writes, and until then it accepts A's 33. The stepper plays it with the numbers from Martin Kleppmann's blog post on locking (he wrote the book Designing Data-Intensive Applications). The ledger in Process pauses was one comparison away from this, because its lease ids grew with every grant.

In Redis, the counter is `INCR fence:{settle}`, which adds one to a number and returns it. The same script that takes the lock runs it, so a token is handed out exactly when a lock is: if `SET ... NX PX` succeeds, return `INCR`, otherwise return 0. The lab's `RedisLock` does that. etcd and ZooKeeper already keep such a number. Every change to etcd gets the next value of one revision counter for the whole cluster. The revision at which a client's lock key was created works as its token. Every change to ZooKeeper gets a zxid, a change number that only grows.

The resource's side is the half people miss, because it isn't lock code at all. In a database table, the write becomes `UPDATE payout_files SET content = :c, fence = :t WHERE batch = :b AND fence <= :t`, which changes this batch's row only if the fence stored in it is no larger than the writer's. Zero rows changed means "you are a late holder". The lab's `PayoutLedger` models that store.

A Redis counter needs two kinds of care. It must never go backwards, so it gets no deadline, and it must live on a Redis that can't throw it away when memory fills up. (Expiry, eviction and memory showed that Redis can be set to throw keys away when memory fills up, and that only the `volatile-*` settings spare keys with no deadline.) And it's only as safe as that one server. Redis copies each change to a spare server, one ready to take over if the main one dies, a moment after it answers (Persistence and replication). If the main server dies before its last increments were copied, the spare takes over without them, and a new holder can get a number that was already handed out. Kleppmann argues that this is why fencing tokens belong to a consensus system such as etcd or ZooKeeper.

His other point is the first question to ask about any lock. Is it for efficiency, so that two servers don't do the same work twice, and a rare double run only costs some processor time or a duplicate email? Or is it for correctness, where a double run pays the shops twice? An efficiency lock can be a single Redis key with a token, like the lock in Caching patterns and stampedes. A correctness lock needs the resource to check something: fencing tokens, or a design where the second run fails anyway, such as a rule in the payouts table that each batch id may appear only once (a unique constraint). The same split sits at the heart of an old argument about a Redis lock spread over five servers. That's next.

stepper.title: Fencing tokens: the store refuses the frozen holder
stepper.intro: Tokens 33 and 34, as in Kleppmann's example. The store stands in for whatever is being written.

frames.say: Take the check away and A's write lands after B's: the file the bank receives is A's out-of-date version, built before B's run, missing 12 shops. The lock kept A and B apart only while A's lease was alive. The token keeps them apart at the one place that sees every write. That's why fencing needs the resource to cooperate: in a database, an `UPDATE ... WHERE fence <= :token`.

try.title: Fence a write by hand
steps: At a Redis prompt (`docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli`), clear the store's hash, set the fence counter to 32, and take two tokens, one for server A and one for server B.

A Redis hash (a value with named fields) plays the payout store here, and the script plays its rule: refuse a fence lower than the one stored. Let B write with its token first, then A with its older one.
Read the stored file. Then, before you run it, predict what A's write would return if B had never written.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.src:
DEL payout:batch-118
SET fence:{settle} 32
INCR fence:{settle}
INCR fence:{settle}
EVAL "local f = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'fence') or '0') if tonumber(ARGV[1]) < f then return 0 end redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'fence', ARGV[1], 'content', ARGV[2]) return 1" 1 payout:batch-118 34 "B: 4210 payouts"
EVAL "local f = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'fence') or '0') if tonumber(ARGV[1]) < f then return 0 end redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'fence', ARGV[1], 'content', ARGV[2]) return 1" 1 payout:batch-118 33 "A: 4198 payouts"
HGETALL payout:batch-118

try.expect: The first `DEL` prints `(integer) 0`, or 1 if an earlier run left the key behind. The two `INCR`s print `(integer) 33` (A's token) and `(integer) 34` (B's). B's write returns `(integer) 1`, and A's returns `(integer) 0`: 33 is lower than the stored 34. `HGETALL` shows `fence` `"34"` and `content` `"B: 4210 payouts"`. Had B never written, A's write would return 1: fencing only refuses a holder once a newer one has written, which is exactly the case that matters.

refs.title: Distributed locks: disclaimer about consistency (Redis docs)

sections.h: Redlock: five Redis servers, and the argument about them
sections.body:
Everything so far used one Redis server, and one server can fail. A spare copy doesn't make the lock safe, because Redis copies each change to the spare a moment after it answers. Server A takes the lock on the main Redis. The main Redis crashes before the change reaches the spare. The spare takes over without the key, and server B takes the same lock. The Redis docs give this exact sequence.

Redlock is Redis's answer. Run several separate Redis servers, usually 5, that copy nothing to each other. To take the lock, a client sends `SET key token NX PX ttl` to all 5 at once, with a short timeout for each. It holds the lock only if at least 3 said yes and the whole attempt took less than the lease. What is left of the lease after the attempt is how long it may hold the lock. If it fails, it releases on all 5.

In 2016 Martin Kleppmann argued that Redlock is unsafe when correctness depends on it. Its safety depends on timing: messages that arrive within a known time, pauses that end within a known time, and clocks that don't jump. If one server's clock jumps forward, its key runs out early, and two clients can each get 3 yes votes. A garbage collection while the replies are on their way leaves a client believing it holds a lock that has already run out. And Redlock has no fencing tokens, because a random value has no order. His advice: for efficiency, a single Redis is enough; for correctness, use a consensus system and fencing.

Salvatore Sanfilippo, known as antirez, who created Redis and designed Redlock, replied within days. He argued that Redlock needs clocks that tick at about the same rate, not clocks that agree. Clock jumps, he said, come from administrators and badly set up time services, which you can avoid. He argued that a pause before the client's final time check is caught by that check, and a pause after it hurts every lock built on leases equally. And he argued that the large random token can be used for a compare-and-set on the resource instead of a counter: write only if the stored value is still the one you expect. He agreed that Redis should use a monotonic clock, one that never jumps, for its deadlines.

Both have a point, and the practical answer has settled. The Redis docs now ask you to read both posts, recommend fencing tokens when correctness matters, and warn that Redis doesn't use a monotonic clock for deadlines. Redisson has deprecated its RedLock object, marking it for removal, in favor of `RLock` and `RFencedLock`, saying the algorithm's safety is disputed. So use a single Redis lock with a token to save work. For correctness, make the resource decide: fencing tokens it checks, a unique constraint, or a lock in the database itself, such as `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, which locks the batch's row until the change is finished (Lost updates: row locks, SKIP LOCKED and job queues). Five Redis servers cost more than either option and settle neither argument.

refs.title: How to do distributed locking (Martin Kleppmann)

compare.title: Take the lock, write with the fence, release: Java and Kotlin

java.title: SettlementJob.java

kotlin.title: SettlementJob.kt

compare.note: Both send the same two scripts to Redis: the acquire script (SET NX PX, then INCR the fence) and the compare-and-delete release. Java repeats the try/finally at every place that takes the lock. Kotlin writes it once, as an inline extension function, a function added to `RedisLock` whose body Kotlin copies into each caller. So a `return` inside the braces returns from `settle`, and no caller can forget the release. Neither version trusts the lock alone. The release in `finally` can't undo a write made after the lease ran out, so the write carries the fence and the store decides. When `write` returns false, the server lost the lock while working and must not report the batch as done.

worked.title: Build the lock one failure at a time

steps.say: First one wins. `NX` creates the key only if it doesn't exist, and Redis runs one command at a time, so exactly one server gets `OK` and the others get nil. It fails the first time a holder crashes: the key never goes away.
Add a deadline inside the same command, and a random token so the holder can prove later that the lock is still its own. Make a fresh UUID for every attempt; never use the server's name.
steps.code:
String token = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
boolean got = redis.set("lock:settle", token, SetParams.setParams().nx().px(30_000)) != null;   // "OK" or null
steps.alt_code:
val token = UUID.randomUUID().toString()
val got = redis.set("lock:settle", token, SetParams.setParams().nx().px(30_000)) != null   // "OK" or null

steps.say: Release only your own lock: compare and delete in one command. On Redis 8.4 and later that's `DELEX`. Before that, it's the three-line Lua script with GET, compare and DEL.
steps.code: boolean released = redis.delex("lock:settle", CompareCondition.valueEq(token)) == 1;   // DELEX ... IFEQ token
steps.alt_code: val released = redis.delex("lock:settle", CompareCondition.valueEq(token)) == 1L   // DELEX ... IFEQ token

steps.say: Number the holders. The acquire becomes a script that adds one to a counter only when the SET succeeded. Every holder gets a larger fence than the one before, and a failed attempt uses up nothing.
steps.code:
if redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[1], 'NX', 'PX', ARGV[2]) then
    return redis.call('INCR', KEYS[2])     -- KEYS[2] = fence:{settle}, no TTL, ever
end
return 0

steps.say: Make the resource check the number. This is the step that protects the data, and it lives in your database, not in Redis: the update succeeds only for a fence at least as large as the last one written.
steps.code:
UPDATE payout_files
   SET content = :content, fence = :fence
 WHERE batch = :batch
   AND fence <= :fence;     -- 0 rows: a newer holder already wrote; stop

lab.title: A Redis lock with tokens and fencing, and the store that enforces it
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All 13 fail. Nine in `RedisLockTest` use a Redis that the tests start in Docker, and four in `PayoutLedgerTest` need no Docker. Leases in the tests really run out, but they're short (200 ms), so a few tests take a fraction of a second.

In `RedisLock.java`, write the `ACQUIRE` script and `tryAcquire`. Run `./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.dist.l05.RedisLockTest'`. Most tests pass now. `a late release does not delete the next holder's lock` still fails: that's the bug in the stub's `release` (the stub is the starting code you were given).
Fix `release` with the `RELEASE` script, and write `extend` with one `SET ... IFEQ`.

In `PayoutLedger.kt`, write `write` with one call to `compute`. Run all 13. The last test in `RedisLockTest` is the stepper from start to end: A's lease runs out during a pause, B writes with a larger fence, and A's late write is refused.
hints: `if redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[1], 'NX', 'PX', ARGV[2]) then return redis.call('INCR', KEYS[2]) end return 0`. The Lua number reaches Java as a `Long`.
`redis.set(key, token, SetParams.setParams().condition(CompareCondition.valueEq(token)).px(ms))` returns null when the condition was false, so `return reply != null;`.
Inside `compute`, return `old` to keep the stored file, or `PayoutFile(fence, content)` to replace it. A `var written = false` outside the lambda records which branch ran.

drill.title: Safe release from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write `release(key, token)` with Jedis twice: once with the compare-and-delete Lua script, and once with the Redis 8.4 command. Then write one sentence on why it can't be a GET in your own code followed by a DEL.

alt.src:
val RELEASE = """
    if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
        return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1])
    end
    return 0
""".trimIndent()

fun release(key: String, token: String): Boolean =
    redis.eval(RELEASE, listOf(key), listOf(token)) == 1L                                 // compare and delete, one command

fun releaseOnRedis84(key: String, token: String): Boolean =
    redis.delex(key, CompareCondition.valueEq(token)) == 1L                              // DELEX key IFEQ token
// GET then DEL is two commands: a pause between them lets the lease expire, and the DEL removes the next holder's lock

recap: A lease is a lock with a deadline, in every lock service: `SET key token NX PX ttl` in Redis, a lease in etcd, a session in ZooKeeper. The service enforces the deadline; nothing makes the holder stop when it passes.
Release with compare-and-delete: a Lua script, or `DELEX key IFEQ token` on Redis 8.4 and later. A plain DEL, or a GET followed by a DEL, can delete the next holder's lock.

Renewing the lease (Redisson's watchdog, 30 seconds by default) covers slow work, not a frozen holder. A lock service built on consensus doesn't help either: Jepsen lost about 18% of the updates guarded by etcd 3.4.3 locks with 2-second leases and pauses.

A fencing token grows with every new holder and travels with every write, and the resource refuses tokens lower than the highest it has seen. It can come from a Redis INCR, etcd's revision or ZooKeeper's zxid.

The limit: a fencing token protects only a resource that checks it, and a Redis counter is only as safe as one server. Redlock spreads the lock over 5 servers, and its safety for correctness is disputed. Use one Redis lock to save work, and fencing or the database itself for correctness.
closing:
We started with three servers and a payout file that must be built once. A lock in Redis keeps them apart while every lease is alive. When a holder freezes past its deadline, only the file store can tell the late write from the current one, by the fencing token it carries.

Look for this in an app you use. Many shared document and wiki tools lock a page while someone edits it. Ask what happens if that person's laptop goes to sleep with the page open: when does the lock run out, and what happens to their edits when the laptop wakes?

Next, we'll put events from different machines in order when no two clocks agree.

quiz.q: Server A releases its lock with `if (token.equals(redis.get(key))) redis.del(key);`. Why is that still unsafe?
options: GET returns a saved copy, not the live value
DEL fails on a key that has a deadline
A pause between the GET and the DEL lets the lease run out and another server take the lock, and the DEL then deletes that server's lock
It is safe: the token check proves the lock is A's
quiz.why: The check and the delete are two commands, and anything can happen between them: a garbage collection, a slow network. The token check was true when it ran and false by the time DEL arrived. A Lua script or `DELEX key IFEQ token` does the compare and the delete inside one command, where nothing can run in between.

quiz.q: From Expiry, eviction and memory: the lock's Redis runs with `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru`, which lets it throw away any key that hasn't been used for a while once memory is full. Memory fills up, and the fence counter `fence:{settle}`, untouched for a day, is thrown away. What happens at the next acquire?
options: INCR starts again from 0 and returns 1, so the store, which has seen 34, refuses every write from now on
INCR fails with an error because the key is gone
Nothing: Redis never throws away keys that have no deadline
The lock can't be taken until someone restores the key
quiz.why: INCR treats a missing key as 0, so the next holder gets 1. The store refuses any fence below 34, so every future batch fails: safe, but stuck until someone fixes the counter. The `allkeys` policies can remove any key; only the `volatile` policies limit themselves to keys with a deadline. A fence counter needs a Redis that never throws it away.

quiz.q: From Process pauses: a holder takes a Redisson lock with the watchdog and calls `isHeldByCurrentThread()` right before each ledger write. Which pause can still let a late write through?
options: None: the watchdog keeps renewing while the JVM is stopped
A pause that starts after the check and outlasts what is left of the lease: the write goes out when the JVM runs again
None: `isHeldByCurrentThread()` asks Redis, so its answer is always current
Only a network failure, never a pause
quiz.why: A stop-the-world pause, a throttled container or a frozen virtual machine stops the watchdog thread along with everything else, so Redis ends the lease on schedule. The check was current when it ran, and a pause right after it is invisible to the holder, exactly as with the careful worker in Process pauses. A network failure is a second way to get there, not the only one. The write must carry a fencing token that the ledger checks.

quiz.q: A team moves the payout lock from Redis to etcd, "because etcd uses consensus", and drops the fencing check. What did Jepsen find when it tested etcd 3.4.3's locks?
options: They were safe: consensus keeps etcd's lock holders apart
They failed only while the network was cut
The store lost confirmed writes, so the locks did too
Even on a healthy cluster, two clients held one lock at the same time within minutes, and a set guarded by the lock lost about 18% of its confirmed updates
quiz.why: etcd's ordinary reads and writes passed, through pauses, crashes, clock jumps and a cut network. Its locks are leases, and a client that freezes past its lease keeps acting while another holds the lock, healthy cluster or not. Network cuts and pauses only made the failures come sooner. Jepsen's advice was to fence each write with the lock key's revision, which is the check the team dropped.

quiz.q: A team runs Redlock on five Redis servers to protect a ledger update and skips fencing, because "a majority makes it safe". What is the strongest objection?
options: Five servers are too slow for payment traffic
A holder can still freeze after taking the lock and write after its lease ended, and Redlock's random value has no order, so the ledger can't tell the late write from the current one
Redlock needs the five servers to copy data to each other, and that copying is delayed
Redlock only works with Redis Cluster
quiz.why: A majority protects taking the lock against one server failing. It can't stop a holder that froze after it got the lock, which is the same failure a single server has. Without a token that grows, the ledger has nothing to compare. Redlock deliberately uses servers that copy nothing to each other, and it doesn't need Redis Cluster, Redis's way of spreading data over many servers.

flashcards.front: Why does every acquire store a fresh random token?
flashcards.back: So the release and the extend can check that the lock is still theirs. A server's name repeats; a fresh UUID for each attempt doesn't.

flashcards.front: What is compare-and-delete on Redis 8.4 and later, and before?
flashcards.back: `DELEX key IFEQ token`. Before 8.4, a Lua script: if GET equals the token then DEL, else return 0.

flashcards.front: What does Redisson's lock watchdog do, and what can't it handle?
flashcards.back: It keeps extending a lock taken without a lease time (`lockWatchdogTimeout`, 30 s by default) while the program runs. It can't help when the whole JVM freezes: it stops too.
A number that grows with every new lock holder and travels with every write. The resource refuses a write whose number is lower than the highest it has accepted.
Efficiency: a double run only wastes work, so one Redis key is fine. Correctness: a double run corrupts data or moves money twice, so the resource must enforce it.

flashcards.front: Where does a fencing token come from in etcd and in ZooKeeper?
flashcards.back: etcd: the revision at which the lock key was created (one revision counter for the whole cluster grows with every change). ZooKeeper: the zxid, a change number that grows with every change.
SET NX PX on 5 separate Redis servers; the lock is held if at least 3 say yes within the lease. Whether it is safe for correctness is disputed.

terms.plain: A permission that only one holder has at a time; the others wait until it's released.
A lock with a deadline: held until it's released or the time runs out, whichever comes first.
A random value the holder stores in the lock key, so only the holder can release or extend it.
Deleting a key only if it still holds an expected value, in one command (`DELEX ... IFEQ` or a Lua script).
A background thread that keeps extending a lock's lease while its holder runs (Redisson's name for it).
A number that grows with each new lock holder; the protected resource refuses writes carrying a lower number.
A number the service increases with every change, so it can serve as a fencing token.
A lock algorithm that takes the same lock on a majority of several separate Redis servers.

explain_back.prompt: Your nightly payout job takes a Redis lock with a 30-second lease and releases it with compare-and-delete. A reviewer asks: "What if the job freezes for 40 seconds?" Explain what happens and what you would change.
explain_back.answer: Redis deletes the lock after 30 seconds, as it should, and nothing tells our job. A second server's SET NX succeeds and it starts the same batch, while ours is frozen by a garbage collection or cut off by the network. When ours wakes up it carries on and writes its payout file, so two servers have written. Compare-and-delete stops us from deleting the second server's lock, but it can't stop our write. Checking the lock before writing doesn't help, because the freeze can fall between the check and the write. A watchdog that renews the lease covers slow work but stops during a freeze like everything else, and moving the lock to etcd or ZooKeeper wouldn't change that: their locks are leases too. So the protection has to sit at the resource. I'd have the acquire script also INCR a fence counter and pass that number to the write, and make the payouts table accept a write only when the fence is at least the last one stored: `UPDATE ... WHERE fence <= :fence`. Zero rows updated tells the job it lost the lock. Since this lock is about not paying shops twice, I'd also add a unique constraint on the batch id, so a second payout file can't be inserted at all.

deeper.body:
**Chubby's sequencers.** Google's Chubby lock service had fencing from the start. A holder asks for a sequencer, a string that names the lock and how many times it has changed hands, and passes it to every server it writes to; the server checks it with Chubby, or against the newest sequencer it has seen. For servers that can't check, Chubby keeps a lock released by a failed holder unavailable for a lock-delay of up to a minute. That narrows the window for a late write without closing it, which is the whole story of Process pauses in one setting.

**The same number under other names.** Raft, a way for machines to agree on a leader and a list of changes, numbers each leader's time in charge with a term. Kafka gives a producer, a program that writes messages, a higher epoch each time it starts again under the same name, and refuses writes from older epochs. Both are fencing tokens, and the Consistency and consensus and Messaging tracks come back to them.

**Locks inside the database.** If the resource is a database, its own locks avoid the problem of two systems entirely. `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` holds a row lock until the transaction ends, and PostgreSQL's advisory locks (`pg_advisory_lock`) give named locks that end with the session. The lock belongs to the same connection as the changes to the data. If the client freezes, the row stays locked and everyone else waits; if its connection dies, the database undoes its transaction and frees the lock. At no moment do two clients both hold it, and no clock decides when it ends.

**Redisson's locks, more closely.** Its `RLock` is a hash whose field is the client's id plus the thread's id, so the same thread can take it again, like a `ReentrantLock`, and only that thread may unlock it. `RFencedLock` (`redisson.getFencedLock(name)`, then `lockAndGetToken()` or `tryLockAndGetToken(...)`) returns a token that grows with every acquisition, like the lab's `RedisLock`. Redisson's docs say the guarded service should accept a token only if it is at least as large as the previous one, the same rule as the lab's `PayoutLedger`.

**Waiting for a lock.** The lab's `tryAcquire` tries once. A loop that retries at a fixed interval makes every waiting server hit Redis at the same moment; retry after a random delay instead, as the Redis docs recommend for Redlock. Redisson's `tryLock(wait, lease, unit)` waits for a message that the lock was released, sent over Redis pub/sub (the Messaging track covers it), instead of asking again and again. etcd and ZooKeeper clients wait by watching the key right ahead of their own.

**Clocks.** Redis computes deadlines from the wall clock, not a monotonic one, so a server whose clock jumps forward ends leases early. The Redis docs mention this in their note on consistency, and it is one more reason, after Clocks you can't trust, to let the time service on lock servers slew the clock (run it a little faster or slower until it's right) rather than step it.
